This moderate reduction aligns with expectations for climate zone 1A, where peak summer cooling loads dominate annual HVAC use. Since attic insulation helps reduce heat gain through the roof, the upgrade improves comfort and reduces energy use, even though the baseline insulation was already moderate. The limited heating season in Florida explains why heating savings were negligible or not observed. This case is a reasonable representation of attic insulation effects in hot-humid climates. It is located in Texas (climate zone 3A), a mixed-humid climate with both heating and cooling needs. Figure 4 shows that the unit uses electricity for both heating and cooling. Cooling energy consumption dropped from 36.6 MBtu to 33.2 MBtu, a 9.3% reduction. These results are consistent with expectations for a mixed climate. The heating savings reflect the low baseline insulation (R-7), which allowed reduction in conductive heat loss during the winter. Meanwhile, cooling savings occurred due to reduced heat gain in summer. The dual-season benefits make this example unit a good representation of attic insulation impacts in mixed-humid zones like 3A. Figure 4. Annual energy consumption for example unit in Texas before and after attic floor insulation upgrade Dwelling unit 3 had baseline attic insulation of R-38 and was upgraded to R-60. It is located in Alaska (climate zone 8AK), the coldest U.S. climate zone, where heating dominates building energy use, and cooling is negligible. Figure 5 shows that this dwelling uses fuel oil for space heating and does not have mechanical cooling. Heating energy use (including fan/pumps) dropped from 56.5 MBtu to 54.1 MBtu, a 4% reduction. The modest savings are expected because the home already had relatively high baseline insulation (R-38), leaving less room for improvement. However, the small but measurable reduction still reflects improved thermal resistance and reduced heat loss through the attic in an extremely cold climate. This example demonstrates diminishing returns for insulation upgrades in homes that are already well- insulated but also highlights the importance of maintaining high performance in severe climates like zone 8AK.
